title: How Dan Osborn Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's Senate campaigns show a different path for Democrats in deep-red states. In places where the party label struggles, an independent with local credibility may perform better than a standard Democratic nominee.
author: gamerdoglover

image.alt: Dan Osborn beside the U.S. Capitol and a Proud Union Home sign

content.text: Dan Osborn has changed how you should think about deep-red Senate races.

Nebraska is not considered a normal Democratic pathway to victory in the 2026 Senate elections. Republicans dominate the state, and Democrats struggle there because the party label carries heavy negative brand recognition. AP has reported that Democrats in several red states are looking toward independents who can outperform the Democratic label.

Osborn is different. He ran as an independent in 2024 and is running again in 2026. He leans on his background as a mechanic, Navy veteran, National Guardsman, and union leader. His campaign focuses on workers' rights, wages, corporate power, and taking money out of politics.

We saw what happened in 2024. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but the race was shockingly close by Nebraska standards. Fischer won by only about six points, while Donald Trump carried the state by more than 20 points. The lesson was simple. Some voters who reject national Democrats may still consider a candidate who sounds local, independent, and focused on economics.

On May 12, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in Nebraska. She campaigned on withdrawing and supporting Osborn. That move reduces the chance of a split anti-Ricketts vote and avoids a three-way race that would likely make the Republican path easier.

Nebraska Democrats appear to understand the basic dynamic. If the race becomes nationalized, Ricketts benefits. If the race becomes local, Osborn has more room to grow. That is what Democrats need to study. Sometimes in a deep-red state, stepping aside is more strategic than forcing the party label onto the ballot.

Of course, this does not work everywhere. The strategy requires a candidate with real local credibility and a message voters believe. It also works better in states with some history of ticket splitting, independent voting, or distrust of both parties. National Democrats also have to stay disciplined. If every independent becomes framed as simply Republican versus not Republican, the independent brand weakens.

Even if the forecast model holds and Osborn loses, the current projected Republican margin of only 3.9 points still sends a message. Democrats cannot keep running the same strategy in deep-red states and expect different results. They need more flexibility, especially in places where the Democratic label starts the race underwater.
The takeaway should be clear. In deep-red states, Democrats may sometimes be better off supporting a candidate who does not run as a Democrat.

Osborn is not the only example. In Montana, Seth Bodnar is staging an independent Senate run after Steve Daines declined to seek reelection and Kurt Alme emerged as the Republican candidate. The Montana Democratic Party has not fully withdrawn its own candidate or embraced Bodnar in the same way Nebraska Democrats have moved around Osborn. That contrast matters. Nebraska shows what a coordinated version of this strategy looks like. Montana shows how messy it can become when the party hesitates.

Alaska offers a different but related lesson. Democrats there have shown that local politics can matter even in a red state. Through coalition politics with moderate Republicans in the state legislature, Democrats have held influence in budget fights and state governance despite Alaska's Republican lean in national races. It is not the same strategy as Osborn's independent campaign, but it points to the same broader idea: localization can make red-state politics less predictable.

Moving into November, Nebraska will either become more competitive or Osborn will lose again. Either way, the strategy has already forced Democrats to rethink how they compete in places where the party brand alone is not enough. In 2026, Nebraska will test whether the Osborn model is just an exception or a real path forward for deep-red states.
